mcqs.question: What's the main trade-off active-active redundancy makes compared to active-passive?
options: Active-active buys near-instant failover and full capacity utilization, at the cost of harder data consistency across simultaneously-active nodes
Active-active is always cheaper because standby capacity is unused
Active-active eliminates the need for health checks entirely
Active-active only works within a single availability zone
mcqs.explanation: Active-active keeps all nodes serving traffic, so failover is fast and hardware isn't idle — but that means multiple nodes can accept writes simultaneously, which raises real consistency challenges. It's not inherently cheaper (idle passive capacity is what's cheap), and it isn't AZ-limited or health-check-free.

mcqs.question: Why does multi-region failover typically have a looser RPO than multi-AZ failover?
options: Multi-region setups never use replication of any kind
Cross-region latency makes synchronous replication impractical, so replication is usually asynchronous, leaving a window of recent data that could be lost
Multi-region failover doesn't use health checks, only manual triggers
RPO isn't a meaningful concept across regions
mcqs.explanation: The physics of cross-region latency push multi-region replication toward asynchronous, which inherently leaves a data-loss window — a looser RPO than same-region synchronous replication can achieve. Multi-region setups do use replication and often do use automated health checks; RPO very much applies, just at a different tier.

mcqs.question: A service needs the fastest possible recovery time and the team is willing to pay continuously to get it. Which DR tier fits?
options: Backup-restore
Pilot light
Multi-site (full-scale active-active)
None — DR tiers don't affect recovery speed
mcqs.explanation: Multi-site active-active keeps full-scale capacity running continuously in more than one location, which is what buys the fastest realistic RTO — at the highest ongoing cost. Backup-restore and pilot light are cheaper but trade away speed, taking hours or tens of minutes respectively.

mcqs.question: Why is a shallow health check (e.g. a bare TCP ping) risky as the trigger for automated failover?
options: It only works for active-passive setups, not active-active
It runs too frequently and overloads the network
It requires manual approval before failing over
It can pass even though the service is failing every real request, leaving traffic routed to a dead instance
mcqs.explanation: A shallow check can produce a false negative for failure — the process responds to a ping while the actual request path (e.g. database queries) is broken — so failover never triggers when it should. This is a correctness problem with the check's depth, not a frequency, approval-flow, or topology issue.

mcqs.question: A team sets DNS TTL to 60 seconds and assumes failover will complete in 60 seconds. What's wrong with that assumption?
options: Not every resolver strictly honors TTL, and client-side caching and stale connections routinely add real delay beyond the configured TTL
TTL has no effect on DNS caching at all
60 seconds is too short a TTL to be valid for any DNS provider
DNS failover doesn't require any TTL configuration
mcqs.explanation: Real-world DNS propagation involves ISP resolvers and clients that don't always respect TTL precisely, plus stale connection pools that keep using an old IP — all of which add delay beyond the textbook TTL number. TTL does affect caching, and 60 seconds is a perfectly valid value; the gap is between configured and actual observed propagation time.

mcqs.question: For a payment service with a strict 5-minute RTO, why would DNS-only multi-region failover likely be ruled out?
options: Because DNS failover is more expensive than any other option
Because DNS propagation and caching delays alone can consume a meaningful chunk of a 5-minute budget, before the new region even starts serving
Because payment services are legally required to use active-passive within one AZ
Because DNS failover cannot be automated
mcqs.explanation: DNS propagation lag is unpredictable and can easily eat several minutes on its own, making it a poor fit when the entire allowed recovery window is 5 minutes. Cost isn't the primary constraint here, there's no such legal requirement, and DNS failover can in fact be automated — the issue is specifically its latency characteristics.
